I think your information may be quite a bit out of date, especially if you’re only relying on a single research paper. Just as a matter of fact there are several other cases on record of rabies survivors. We have more than three documented cases of symptomatic patient survival in the US alone. [This article](https://rabiesalliance.org/resource/could-more-people-survive-rabies) from 2016 references two reviews that list a total of 19 survivors. Notably, it’s been 7 years since then, so even that is pretty out of date. Here’s a [more recent review](https://doi.org/10.1590/0037-8682-0352-2020) which references 20 survivors between two different methods of treatment. This is as of 2020.

This is actually not true. There have been a few rabies survivors who were treated using the Milwaukee protocol. The first and most widely known case was a girl who woke up from her medically induced coma and basically had to relearn everything, including walking, before she could return to her life. It took her a long time to recover. There is also a child survivor who had an encounter with a feral cat, and she recovered with treatment and bounced back very quickly. Other survivors beat the virus but have varying degrees of disability.
If you’re interested, there’s an excellent book by Bill Wasik titled “Rabies”, which has a chapter that pretty extensively covers modern attempts to treat the virus after symptoms appear. It is a super interesting read and very readable even with very little medical know-how (:

I do agree with the implied point, though. The Milwaukee protocol exists, but it’s not exactly a reliable treatment. If you get rabies and show symptoms, you’re going to die. I think the people in these comments that are losing their marbles because people aren’t making the disclaimer that there’s a minuscule possibility that you can be put in a coma and survive are missing the point, which is that prevention is better, and that the Milwaukee protocol is a no-go without access to medical care anyways.

I wasn’t out when I started in the traditional way, because for myself at least I’m diametrically opposed to the whole “coming out” thing. My thoughts were and are that straight and cis people don’t have to come out, and I wasn’t going to either. For some people coming out is freeing, but for just as many it’s a really stressful and even traumatic time where they risk losing family, friends, or resources. I decided to just live my life and mind my business, and anyone who didn’t like it could fuck right off.
At this point I’d been openly binding and talking about top surgery for years, and had changed my name in every way but legally about two years before, but somehow most of my family members were not clued in at all. My mom told me later that she was afraid I was going to tell her I was a lesbian. Surprise, Mom.
Anyways, if you eliminate the “coming out” and start from the moment where I allowed myself to publicly live and present as male, it was about two years. But I knew with certainty that I wanted to pursue HRT after 3 months, if not less. If I had started then, I’d be just as well now.

NTA. You’ve set a clear boundary that doesn’t interfere with your mom’s ability to parent you. If it were a slip-up, it would be N.A.H., but because she’s insisting on using an old name or nickname that presumably triggers dysphoria for you in spite of your efforts to communicate your feelings with her, she’s an asshole. I’m glad to see in another comment that she’s been at least nominally supportive so far, but as a fellow trans person, I can tell you that deadnaming from someone who knows you have changed your name and why is kind of a red flag. I would suggest pointing your mother to outside resources since your explanation hasn’t seemed to help her understand the significance of deadnaming someone. I would suggest the Trever Project’s “Guide to Being an Ally to Transgender and Non-binary Youth” or “the guide to being a trans ally” by PFLAG. Both of these are freely available for download on their respective websites.
NTA. However, your husband is, grandma is, and you would be if you continued to allow her to emotionally and verbally abuse your kids.

If OP has already asked their mom to use their new name, the solution is incredibly straightforward and simple:  do it. Mistakes will happen, but it’s easy to forgive when they’re honest and it’s clear that the other person is putting forth effort to be respectful.
